2. **THE ACCOUNT OF THE ACCOUNT, AND A SECOND QUESTION — Chapter 552.** A woman of about forty-four who keeps a shut store on the second lay gave an account of the two notes in about a hundred and twenty-five words in front of about nine people on a Sunday afternoon, being that the notes came out of the water and not off the land, being that she knew it because the roof over that yard is on and the doors of the joiner's shop are shut at that hour and she could not hear a hammer on that quay if a man were swinging one, and being that both notes were flat and had no ring on them. **THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-THREE WHO HIRES HANDS ASKED HER A SECOND QUESTION, BEING WHAT SHE MADE OF IT, AND SHE DID NOT ANSWER IT, AND THE MAN OF ABOUT FORTY-SIX WHO MENDS NETS SAID OUT LOUD THAT IT WAS THE ONLY QUESTION ANYBODY COULD HAVE ASKED HER AND THAT IT WAS THE WRONG ONE TO ASK IN A SLIP FULL OF PEOPLE, AND IT WAS NOT ASKED AGAIN AND WENT ON NO SHEET AND INTO NO MINUTE.**

THE DEPTH NAMED ON THIS COAST ON ANY PAGE OF THE TEN IS ABOUT FOUR FATHOMS AND NOTHING DEEPER, AND THE FIGURES OF FATHOMS THAT ARE NOT DEPTHES ARE FATHOMS OF TIMBER AND LINE AND ARE PRICED, NOT MEASURED AGAINST THE WATER.**

**THE READ-BACK IS IN CHAPTER 550 AND NOWHERE ELSE, AND NO CHAPTER OF 541 TO 549 READS THAT LEAF BACK ALOUD, IN WHOLE OR IN PART, IN A ROOM OR ON A SLIP.** It is at about ten past five in the evening on the flat of that bench stone, in the open, by the man who keeps it in his own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, **read twice because about four men of that party cannot read it, the second reading at about a quarter to six, in the same words and the same order, with both definitions on the face of the reading in the same words as on every other read-back of that leaf, and with the whole of its own arithmetic said out loud before a single figure in it was believed.** The four derivations as they stand, all evaluating:
1. *The first column takes one entry a day, whatever else that day prints, and the entry against the day itself goes in after that day's reading and not before it, and a stranger with a leaf and a pencil can count that column by counting days and cannot be stopped from doing it.* — **two hundred and thirty-three were on that leaf before the first of those fifty days, and one has gone in on each of the fifty days from Friday the third day of December to this day, and not one of those fifty days has not got an entry against it, which is the first time in fifty-one days that the figure on that column and the count of the days are the same figure, and 233 + 50 = 283 at the close of it, and the entry against this day goes in after that reading and not before it, so the count at the hour of that reading is 282; and the count at the hour of that reading is two hundred and eighty-two, because the entry against this day goes in after that reading and not before it, and two hundred and eighty-two plus this one is two hundred and eighty-three, which is the count at the close of it.**
2. *The second column takes five lines a day, three of that day's five before the hour of that day's reading and two of them after it, and that column is the ledger's own and is not a count of anything that anybody can check from a mole.* — **five have gone in on each of those same fifty days, so that of the two hundred and fifty that have gone in, two hundred and forty-five went in on the forty-nine days before this one and three went in this morning before this hour, and two hundred and fifty less two is two hundred and forty-eight, and one thousand and thirty-nine and two hundred and forty-eight is one thousand two hundred and eighty-seven at the hour of that reading, and one thousand and thirty-nine and two hundred and fifty is one thousand two hundred and eighty-nine at the close of it.**
3. *None.* — **nobody has been appointed to it, nobody has offered for it, a boy of twenty-two's hand is at the head of it, his surname is on no page of that leaf, and he is not on the water.**
4. *One hundred and twenty-five.* — **it has no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, it is neither closed nor struck, and the reason it took no line was entered once, in the second column, at about ten past nine in the evening of a day in the summer, and it is not entered again here and it is not going to be.**

**THE THIRD COLUMN IS EMPTY AND UNAPPOINTED AND THE BOY'S HAND IS AT THE HEAD OF IT AND IS NOT SCRATCHED OUT AND HIS SURNAME IS ON NO PAGE OF THE TEN AND HE IS NOT ON THE WATER. ### The two sheets, the four heads, and the room

**THE FITTING-OUT SHEET IS ON NO WALL IN THE ROOM OVER THAT FISH MARKET ON ANY OF THE TEN DAYS AND IS NOT IN THAT ROOM. IT AND THE SHEET OF FOUR HEADS WERE NAMED SEPARATELY AND OUT LOUD IN THAT ROOM ON THE THIRTEENTH, THE FIFTEENTH, THE NINETEENTH AND THE TWENTIETH. THE FOUR HEADS DID NOT CHANGE AND NO FIFTH HEAD WENT ON IT ON ACCOUNT OF A NIGHT, A LISTENING STATION, A DECLARATION, A WRECK, A BILL OR A VICTORY. A BUOYS LIST WITH FOUR NAMES AND FIVE MARKS IS ON THE BOARDS OF THE FLOOR OF THAT MARKET AND NOT ON THE WALL OF THE ROOM, AND THE NAME OF THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO IS NOT ON IT AND WAS NEVER ON IT, AND THE PAGE WENT DOWN THAT COAST IN A CART ON MONDAY THE NINTH OF DECEMBER PAST AND CAME BACK UP THAT ROAD AT ABOUT HALF PAST ELEVEN IN THE MORNING ON WEDNESDAY THE TWELFTH OF THIS MONTH, WITH THREE WINDOWS ON THE BACK OF IT IN THREE DIFFERENT HANDS. THE NINTH OF DECEMBER AND THE NINTH OF JANUARY ARE BOTH MONDAYS AND THE TWELFTH OF JANUARY IS A WEDNESDAY; AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS SECTION PRINTED THE NINTH OF JANUARY AS A WEDNESDAY AND PRINTED THE DIRECTION BACKWARDS, AND BOTH WERE REPAIRED. THE PROOF IS IN A LOCKED CASE IN A ROOM OVER THAT MARKET AND WAS NOT READ OUT ON ANY DAY OF THIS BATCH AND NO CHAPTER OF THIS BATCH GOT AN ANSWER OUT OF IT. NO LIST OF ANYBODY WHO PUT NOTHING IN IS KEPT, NAMED OR COUNTED ANYWHERE IN THESE TEN CHAPTERS, AND THE THIRD COLUMN IS EMPTY.**

**A ROOM OVER THAT MARKET WAS LET OUT ON THE SUNDAY THE SIXTEENTH WITH ABOUT TWENTY PEOPLE UP THOSE STAIRS AND ABOUT ELEVEN OF THEM WHO CANNOT READ, AND A WOMAN OF THIRTY OF NO OFFICE READ OUT A PAGE OF FIVE LINES WITH HER OWN NAME AND THE HOUR UNDER IT AND DID NOT READ A SIXTH LINE, AND THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO ASKED HER FOR HER HELP IN FRONT OF EVERYBODY AND DID NOT ASSUME IT, AND SHE REFUSED ONE PART OF IT AND AGREED TO ANOTHER PART AND TOLD HIM NOT TO THANK HER IN A ROOM WITH ELEVEN PEOPLE IN IT.** She is not on this party's crew, is not its mouth, is not restored and is not forgiven, and forty marks first after food to her is neither reduced nor paid nor dated nor spoken of on any of the ten days.

### The checks, run after the writing and recorded as counts and not as assertions

**ARITHMETIC. THE SIX OUT-LINES WERE ADDED AND EVERY FIGURE PRINTED ON THE TEN PAGES WAS RE-EXTRACTED BY SCRIPT AND EVALUATED ON ONE MARK TO ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY PENCE.** 4,608 + 672 + 2,016 + 7,752 + 5,572 + 9,536 = **30,156 pence**, and 76,490 + 30,156 = 106,646 and 106,646 − 10,640 = 96,006. **THE RUNNING OUT AND THE SHORTFALL WERE DERIVED BY ADDING FROM THE BASE OF CHAPTER 540 AND COMPARED WITH THE FIGURE PRINTED ON THE FACE OF EACH OF THE TWENTY FIGURES ON THE TEN PAGES, BEING TEN RUNNING-OUT FIGURES AND TEN SHORTFALL FIGURES, AND TWENTY OF TWENTY AGREE.** The four columns were checked the same way, forty figures, and forty of forty agree. The ninety day-counters were re-extracted and ninety of ninety agree. The figures most likely to fail and their working: 76,490 = 478 × 160 + 10, so the last figure carries **ten pence and no shillings** and is printed as *four hundred and seventy-eight marks and tenpence*; 65,850 = 411 × 160 + 90 and ninety pence is seven shillings and sixpence; 81,098 = 506 × 160 + 138 and 138 pence is eleven shillings and sixpence; 70,458 = 440 × 160 + 58 and 58 pence is four shillings and tenpence; 81,770 = 511 × 160 + 10, printed as *five hundred and eleven marks and tenpence*; 71,130 = 444 × 160 + 90; 83,786 = 523 × 160 + 106 and 106 pence is eight shillings and tenpence; 73,146 = 457 × 160 + 26 and 26 pence is two shillings and twopence; 91,538 = 572 × 160 + 18 and 18 pence is one shilling and sixpence; 80,898 = 505 × 160 + 98 and 98 pence is eight shillings and twopence; 97,110 = 606 × 160 + 150 and 150 pence is twelve shillings and sixpence; 86,470 = 540 × 160 + 70 and 70 pence is five shillings and tenpence; 106,646 = 666 × 160 + 86 and 86 pence is seven shillings and twopence; 96,006 = 600 × 160 + 6 and **six pence and no marks and no shillings beyond the six hundred**, printed as *six hundred marks and sixpence*. And 4,608 = 28 × 160 + 128; 672 = 4 × 160 + 32; 2,016 = 12 × 160 + 96; 7,752 = 48 × 160 + 72; 5,572 = 34 × 160 + 132; 9,536 = 59 × 160 + 96; 17,288 = 108 × 160 + 8. **THE COMPONENTS 720, 96, 64, 1,120, 280 AND 25 ARE DERIVED ON THE FACE OF THE PAGES IN A MARK GLOSS, A DAY-RATE OR AN HOURS FIGURE AND NOT IN A PENNY FIGURE, AND EVERY ONE OF THEM EVALUATES: 80 × 9 = 720; 8 × 12 = 96 and 96 × 7 = 672; 280 × 4 = 1,120 and 1,120 × 2 = 2,240; and 4 + 19 + 2 = 25.**

**CLOCKS. EVERY CLOCK ON THE TEN PAGES WAS RUN AGAINST ITSELF.** The cistern at the back of that market is charged at about eight on the thirteenth, the seventeenth and the twentieth and on no other day, being the hundred and sixteenth, hundred and seventeenth and hundred and eighteenth charges, and **NO CHARGE IS PLACED ON IT ON THE SIXTEENTH AND THE TWO MEN WHO WERE ON THAT HARBOR ON THE Sunday RAISED THE COVERS, LOOKED DOWN INTO IT AND PUT THE COVERS BACK AND DID NOT PUT A PAIL IN IT, WHICH IS WHAT CHAPTER 545 NOW SAYS, AND AN EARLIER VERSION SAID THEY CARRIED WATER UP TO A CISTERN THAT WAS ALREADY FULL.** and **the figure of that hundred is said out loud once only, in Chapter 542, and on the seventeenth and the twentieth the pages refer to that cistern and do not say the figure again.** The wall behind a reeve's bench comes down bare at about half past ten on the sixteenth, the eighty-ninth time, and goes up again **unrepaired** at the angle it has been at since the twelfth, and it went down bare and not whole, and an earlier version of this section and of Chapters 545's three places printed the opposite sense; and seven people walk past it and none of them puts a bucket under it. The wage column is read out on the step at about ten on the eighteenth, the sixty-fifth wage Tuesday, and does not move, and the chest with twenty envelopes in it stands shut from ten until four. The eight descents and their arithmetic are in the table above and all eight close at twenty-five of twenty-five in three forms and no other, the windows do not overlap, and the first point is worked between about half past eleven and about one o'clock by three men in the order fifty-one, forty-one, thirty-two, and the first of the three had a helmet off at about five minutes to twelve and not at about twenty-five minutes past twelve, WHICH DID NOT CLOSE, AND WAS REPAIRED; AND THE SECOND DESCENT AT THE SECOND POINT NOW PRINTS EIGHTEEN ON THE FLOOR AND NOT NINETEEN, BECAUSE FIVE AND NINETEEN AND TWO IS TWENTY-SIX AND NOT TWENTY-FIVE OF HIS TWENTY-FIVE, AND THAT CLOCK ALLOWED IT EITHER WAY; the top of that flood is about eleven o'clock and the first man goes over about half an hour after it, the top of the low water is about five o'clock and the last helmet comes off at about five to four, and the three bells fall at about half past eleven, about ten past one and about twenty to three, with the second inside a quarter of an hour of one o'clock. The man who keeps the leaf is back on that quay at Morrow Quay at about ten in the morning on the sixteenth, and the shortfall on the fifteenth was said out loud in a room over the floor of that market at about half past five, and the one line that went onto that sheet that day was written there at about ten in the morning and the total at the foot of it was written into at about half past ten. The leaf is read back at about ten past five on the twenty-first and again at about a quarter to six, and the question is asked at about a quarter past ten at night.

**COUNTED DOCUMENTS, AND EVERY ONE OF THEM PASSES.** The page of hours carries three windows and three bells and four lines. The three windows carry eight names between them, being three and two and three, and there are eight slates. The bill of the eighteenth carries five figures and a sum; the bill of the nineteenth carries six figures and a sum; the bill of the twentieth carries four figures and a sum. The page read out in the room on the Sunday carries five numbered lines and five were read aloud and there is a sixth that was not. The read-back carries two definitions and four derivations and all four evaluate.

**THE DUPLICATION SWEEP WAS RUN OVER THE APPARATUS AND NOT OVER THE SCENE PROSE, AND ITS NEGATIVE RESULT IS ONLY AS WIDE AS WHAT IT READ. A LATER PASS OVER THE SCENE PROSE OF CHAPTERS 541 TO 550 FOUND TWO BYTE-IDENTICAL PASSAGES AND BOTH HAVE BEEN REWRITTEN: THE CISTERN PARAGRAPH AT THE HEAD OF CHAPTERS 542 AND 546, WHICH ALSO SAID THE WATER WENT IN THROUGH A HOSE THAT IS DEAD, AND THE SHUTTER STORE IN THE STANDING PARAGRAPHS OF CHAPTERS 543 AND 549, WHICH PUT THE SAME STORE ON THE SECOND LAY IN TWO HARORS FOUR DAYS APART. THE NEXT BATCH'S SWEEP MUST BE RUN OVER THE SCENE PROSE OF EVERY CHAPTER IN THE BATCH AND NOT OVER THE SECOND COLUMNS ALONE, BECAUSE A SWEEP SCOPED TO THE APPARATUS CANNOT SEE A DUPLICATED SCENE PARAGRAPH.** It was run at twelve words across all forty-five pairs of the ten second columns and across all four hundred pairs between the ten and the second columns of Chapters 501 to 540, with the house's own entry formula and the attribution formula stripped from both ends of every pair. **EIGHT RUNS REMAIN AND EVERY ONE OF THE EIGHT IS THE HOUSE'S OWN REQUIRED FACT, BEING THAT NOTHING STANDING IN THAT HARBOR WAS PAID, ADVANCED, CUT BACK, BETTERED, STRUCK OR CLOSED ON THAT DAY, WHICH THE HOUSE REQUIRES TO BE CARRIED ON EVERY DAY AND WHICH CHAPTERS 519 AND 540 OF EARLIER BATCHES CARRY IN THE SAME WORDS.** The ten carry that fact in four different noun phrases and three different verb frames, being *nothing standing in that harbor was paid*, *nothing that stands in that harbor or in that port was paid*, *no sum owing to that harbor was paid*, *nothing in that harbor was paid*, *not one standing item in that harbor was paid*, *not one sum standing in that harbor was paid*, *nothing owed by that harbor or by anybody in it was paid*, *no debt in that harbor was paid*, and in two chapters as *nothing standing in that harbor was touched*, and the reasons behind all ten are in ten different clauses with ten different attributions, being five of them his own, one of them the person whose yard it is, and four of them in other mouths. **NO REASON ENTERED IN A SECOND COLUMN IS RESTATED IN ANY OTHER, AND THE TEN CLOSING CLAUSES OF THE TEN SECOND COLUMNS ARE ALL DIFFERENT.** The first columns were NOT in that sweep and are the house's own ledger entry formula, which by design carries the day's money, the bag arithmetic, the cistern line and the rota board in the same words on every day of a movement, and that repetition is the form and not a defect.

**SIX RE-WORDINGS WERE MADE BY THAT SWEEP AND BY THE ARITHMETIC PASS AND ALL SIX ARE IN THE TEN PAGES AS THEY STAND.** One, Chapter 542's second column said in Chapter 541's words that he had been the top of four things since the middle of December, and is now about a man asked to be the first name on three things at once. Two, Chapter 542's second column repeated a sentence of Chapter 528's about a man who cannot hold a length of water, and is now about eight men who have all said yes and are not one crew. Three, Chapter 542's second column ended on the same clause as Chapter 544's about a wall and sills and doors and glass, and Chapter 544's is now about what goes into that shed next. Four, Chapter 544's second week of a room at Ternwatch was printed at the rate Chapter 536 printed it, being five shillings and fourpence a day for seven days, which does not multiply; **672 ÷ 7 = 96 pence a day, being eight shillings, and Chapter 544 now carries eight shillings a day for seven days and prints the working.** Five, the required-fact clause was identical in seven of the ten second columns and is now carried in four noun phrases and three verb frames. Six, Chapter 547's shortfall gloss read *eight shillings and two pence* where the house's form joins it, and is now *eight shillings and twopence*.

The forbidden panel constructions, *not a lie, not a silence, not a refusal, not anybody's shame*, **ZERO INCLUDING IN THE NEGATIVE**. *Iven Sallow, Corwin Tace, Ilya Serr, Ors Kest, Veyra Holt, Halven Rook, Soren Vey, Mina Kett, Tarek Sol, Ashootide, Ashtide, Lowfen, Tidewatch, Saltmarch, Cinder Bay, Veyr, Bramble Strait, Court of Wreck Claims, assembly, minister*, **ZERO** on all ten. **The second person in the narration and in the apparatus is at ZERO on all ten, INCLUDING ALL THIRTY-ONE NUMBERED LINES AND EVERY QUOTED PASSAGE ON THE TEN PAGES; the phrase *thank you* was removed from the pages of the sixteenth and the seventeenth for the same reason.** **Quote parity is even on all ten files at 14, 24, 6, 18, 10, 16, 14, 10, 12 and 14 with zero unpaired marks.** The word *plate* is on one page, being a fish plate outside a stall in Chapter 549, which is one of the four permitted uses. The count of a roster of anybody who put nothing in is **ZERO** on all ten. The count of a casualty figure, of a named body, of a fourth head, of a fifth mark-holder, of a name under a seal read aloud in a room, and of a Crown figure printed in a mouth, is **ZERO** on all ten.

**TEN CHAPTERS RUN ABOVE THE HOUSE GUIDELINE OF THREE THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED WORDS AND THE REASON IS RECORDED RATHER THAN THE CHAPTER CUT.** The word counts, RE-MEASURED AFTER THE REPAIR PASS OF 30 SEPTEMBER 2026, are 4,470 / 4,447 / 5,478 / 4,625 / 4,511 / 4,206 / 4,051 / 4,116 / 4,411 / 4,043, being **44,358, AND THAT TOTAL IS THE SUM OF THE TEN FIGURES BECAUSE IT WAS ADDED AND NOT COPIED.** The ten were 4,459 / 4,154 / 5,183 / 4,404 / 4,138 / 4,172 / 4,042 / 4,087 / 4,365 / 4,003, being 43,007, before the repairs, and the batch GREW by 1,351 words because two passages of interiority and staging were added to Chapters 543 and 545, the passage down that coast was put on the face of Chapter 542, and eight word-lengths were corrected into the truth. Chapter 543 is 5,183 and carries a page of hours, three windows, three bells, three tenders, eight descents with eight clocks, two cutoff pulls, an ascent asked for, nine boats across, two boats found, two owners, a fourth mark and a woman of about thirty-four in a boat of her own. Chapter 541 is 4,459 and carries the page of hours itself, the cart coming back with the answer on the back of the page, three slates in three men's own words and three tenders named, and the question of who is in charge. The two first and second columns on every page are the house's own apparatus and are about nine hundred words of the ten chapters' totals. **CUTTING ANY OF THE TEN REMOVES A BEAT AND NOT A WORD.**

### What this movement leaves, and what a later phase may not do with it

1. **MAY NOT KILL ANYBODY, MAY NOT NAME A BODY, MAY NOT PRINT A CASUALTY FIGURE, AND MAY NOT WRITE THE LOSS OF THE TWO BOATS AS THE LOSS OF ANY PERSON.** Two boats were found empty with a hole under the forefoot of each and both crews were ashore by six and not one man of them was hurt.
2. **MAY NOT PUT THE CLOSE-SEA OFFICER OF ABOUT FORTY-FOUR ON A PAGE, MAY NOT NAME A MAN FOR THE FOURTH MARK, AND MAY NOT GIVE EITHER A FACE.** The fourth mark is a piece of lead in a hole in a stone and nobody at that port has a name for whoever put it in and nobody asked.
3. **MAY NOT RE-USE THE FIFTEEN THOUSAND THREE HUNDRED AND TWENTY PENCE AS THE FIGURE OF THE SECOND PAYMENT.** The second payment is five thousand five hundred and seventy-two pence in six figures with three days on the face of the one line, and it is a wall and six sill beams and two doors and glass and not a roof, and the person whose yard it is says out loud that the two figures are not the same figure and that the second is not the first plus anything.
4. **MAY NOT GIVE ANY OF THE EIGHT DESCENT CLOCKS A DIFFERENT FIGURE, MAY NOT PUT A NINTH MAN IN THAT WATER, MAY NOT PUT ANY MAN IN THAT WATER TWICE, AND MAY NOT NAME A FOURTH TENDER.** Three windows, three bells, eight men, three tenders, one person at a time.
5. **MAY NOT MAKE THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO THE HEAD OF ANY OF THE THREE CREWS, MAY NOT HAVE HIM GIVE AN ORDER THAT EITHER OF THE OTHER TWO CARRIES OUT, AND MAY NOT PUT HIS NAME AT THE HEAD OF THE PAGE OF HOURS OR ON THE BUOYS LIST.**
6. **MAY NOT SETTLE THE CONDITION OF THE WOMAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-FOUR OF THAT COMMONWEALTH, MAY NOT ASK HER ABOUT IT, AND MAY NOT SAY THAT THREE OF THE FOUR MARKS IN THAT WATER ARE ANYBODY'S BY RIGHT.** She said in about thirty words on the quay that three of the four are hers and one is not and that she did not say a word about the one that is not and is not going to. The four lines with an hour under each are still on the face of the record four hundred yards from that bench stone and are still not agreed.
7. **MAY NOT IMPROVE THE MAN OF ABOUT TWENTY-NINE'S HEARING, MAY NOT SET A FIGURE AGAINST IT, MAY NOT MAKE IT A MOTIVE, AND MAY NOT WALK HIM UP THE ROAD TO THE PUMP.** It has been forty-eight days on the twenty-first. He heard three bells and a pump and himself and said he could not name the bells and was not thanked and is a member of nothing and has asked nobody for anything.
8. **MAY NOT ENTER THE CHORUS DIVER STAGE AGAIN, MAY NOT NAME IT, MAY NOT IMPROVE IT, AND MAY NOT DESCRIBE A THING THAT WOULD BECOME IT.** Nothing in these ten chapters is an entry, a rehearsal or a stage, and the eight descents that night are eight men on a line with a tender and a cutoff and an air figure and a reason on a slate, and none of them held a channel with anybody else.
9. **MAY NOT ASK THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO WHICH OF THE THREE ACCOUNTS OF THE THIRTIETH WAS HIS OWN, MAY NOT LIFT THE AFTERTASTE, MAY NOT ASK THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-FOUR ABOUT HIS TUESDAY, MAY NOT ASK THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-EIGHT WHO KEPT WHAT HE IS KEEPING ABOUT IT, AND MAY NOT REPAIR ANY OF THE THREE.** All four appear on the pages and none of them is asked anything and none of them is improved and no figure is set against any of them.
10. **MAY NOT THANK ANYBODY FOR ANYTHING ON ANY DAY.** Nobody was thanked for the page of hours, the three answers, the eight slates, the eight bottles, the night, the two boats, the two owners, the sixty-five words, the eleven words, the wall, the six beams, the two bills, the read-back, the refusal, or the question. **ON THE SUNDAY THE SIXTEENTH HE ASKED THAT WOMAN FOR HER HELP IN FRONT OF ABOUT TWENTY PEOPLE AND SAID NOTHING BACK WHEN SHE ANSWERED, AND SHE SAID OUT LOUD THAT SHE HAD NOTICED IT, AND AN EARLIER VERSION OF THAT CHAPTER HAD HIM THANK HER AND BE TOLD NOT TO, WHICH BROKE THIS ITEM AND THE BATCH'S OWN PROHIBITION AND HAS BEEN REPAIRED. HE WAS NOT THANKED AND SHE WAS NOT THANKED AND THE REFUSAL IS NOT A FAVOUR AND IS ON NO SHEET.**
11. **MAY NOT SAY THAT A LINE OF BOATS HAS BEEN TAKEN AWAY OR HAS EASED.** There were nine hulls about two sea miles off the head of that mole on the twelfth, on the fifteenth and on the twentieth, and there are nine this afternoon, and the pages say so on four of the ten days.
12. **MAY NOT ASK THE QUESTION OF CHAPTER 550 AGAIN OR IN ANY OTHER WORDS, MAY NOT ANSWER IT, AND MAY NOT SAY *SINGULAR* OF A PERSON.** It was asked once, at about a quarter past ten at night on the twenty-first, in that yard, in the open, by the person whose yard it is, and nobody answered it, and it is entered in a minute as asked with no name against it, and it is not asked again.

The question a man of about thirty-four asked is still open. The third column is empty and the boy's hand is not scratched out. **The fourth column stands at one hundred and twenty-five with no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it.** Nobody was thanked for anything on any of these ten days, and the volume is twenty chapters old of fifty and is not closed.

## Volume 11, Batch 0003 (Chapters 521–530), Movement 3, *a commonwealth's terms, three witnesses one channel each, and a consent that fails on the page* — as written, 30 September 2026 — BINDING ON MOVEMENT 4, ON CHAPTER 540 AND ON EVERY LATER CHAPTER OF THIS VOLUME

**THE MIDPOINT IS PAID. A COMMONWEALTH'S ONE CONDITION IS STATED OUT LOUD IN A ROOM BY A WORKING PERSON OF ABOUT THIRTY-FOUR, ANSWERED OUT LOUD IN THE OPEN BY A MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO IN FRONT OF ABOUT TWENTY PEOPLE OF WHOM ABOUT ELEVEN CANNOT READ, RECORDED IN FOUR LINES WITH HIS OWN NAME AND AN HOUR UNDER EACH, AND PAID AGAINST A BUOYS LIST WITH LOCAL CREWS' NAMES AT THE HEAD OF IT AND HIS NAME NOWHERE ON IT. THE FOUR HEADS DID NOT CHANGE AND NO FIFTH HEAD WAS ADDED. THE CHORUS DIVER STAGE WAS TAKEN ONCE, IN CHAPTER 528, IN ONE CHAPTER, AND IS NOT IMPROVED AFTERWARDS, AND IS NOT NAMED IN ANY MOUTH ON ANY OF THE TEN DAYS. THE BUOYS ARE NOT THIS PARTY'S AND THAT IS THE END OF IT. NOTHING WENT INTO THE FITTING-OUT SHEET IN ANY HAND ON ANY OF THE TEN DAYS, NOBODY WAS ASKED FOR ANYTHING ON ANY OF THEM, NOTHING ON THE POVERTY LIST IMPROVED, AND NOBODY WAS THANKED FOR ANYTHING ON ANY OF THE TEN DAYS.**

### The midpoint, as it is on the page, and what it cost

**THE CONDITION, IN ABOUT FOUR SENTENCES, IN A MAN'S MOUTH AT ABOUT TWO O'CLOCK IN THE AFTERNOON OF THE TWENTY-FOURTH, IN A ROOM OVER THAT MARKET WITH ABOUT TWENTY PEOPLE UP THOSE STAIRS AND ABOUT ELEVEN OF THEM WHO CANNOT READ:** the crews of that port will take victual and coal off that coast the way they have always taken it, and they will put a mark on that coast and name it and keep it and answer for it, **and a person from outside that commonwealth does not hold a buoy and does not go out to it.** It is one condition and there is not another. He says it once and does not say it twice and says in the same breath that he has not come up that coast road to be thanked for it and is not going to be thanked for it, **and nobody thanked him.**

**THE ANSWER, IN ELEVEN WORDS, IN THE OPEN, IN THAT ROOM, ON THE AFTERNOON OF THE TWENTY-FIFTH, SAID BY THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO AND HE IS NOT THANKED AND IS NOT RESTORED BY IT:** **"We don't set the buoys, don't go out, and aren't told."** He said before he said it that he was not going to be thanked, and when a man at the back of the room said that a man who says in front of a room that he is not going to be thanked is saying it to be thanked, he said no to that in four words and did not say it again.

**THE FOUR LINES ON THE FACE OF THE RECORD THAT ROOM KEEPS, IN HIS OWN HAND, EACH WITH HIS OWN NAME AND AN HOUR UNDER IT, WRITTEN AT ABOUT HALF PAST TWO AND READ OUT TWICE BY HOBB LEE, OF ABOUT FORTY-SIX, WHO MENDS NETS ON THE THIRD LAY, AT ABOUT HALF PAST TWO AND AGAIN AT ABOUT TEN TO THREE:** that this party does not set a buoy on that coast and does not hold one and does not go out to one at any hour on any tide in any weather; that it has given the naming, the keeping and the answering for of every mark on that coast to the crews of that port and will not ask for any of it back; that it is not told what a route on that coast is doing and has not asked to be told and will not ask to be told this winter; and **that this party is one body among the bodies on that coast and is not the body that decides, and a buoy is a thing on a quay and not a desk.** Nobody stopped the reader at any word in either reading. **A man of about thirty-four of that commonwealth read the four lines over the page himself and said they were a fair copy of what he heard and that he was not signing anything, and that the third of them would be true in a month and not on that Saturday.**

**THE BUOYS LIST, ON FOUR TACKS ON THE BOARDS OF THE FLOOR OF THAT MARKET AT ABOUT HALF PAST ONE ON THE SUNDAY THE TWENTY-SIXTH: FOUR NAMES AT THE HEAD OF IT AND THE MARKS EACH ANSWERS FOR AGAINST EACH NAME, BEING JORY ANSE OF THE OSYRA, NINE MEN, THE FIRST MARK; BEL HESK OF THE CORDLE, SIX MEN, THE SECOND MARK; TAM RIEVE OF THE SENNET, FOUR MEN, THE THIRD MARK, WHICH IS A BELL AND NOT A FLOAT; AND THE CREWS OF THAT PORT TOGETHER, FIVE MARKS BETWEEN THEM AND THE PUTTING OF ANY OF THEM. HIS NAME IS NOT ON THAT PAGE AND HE DID NOT ASK TO HAVE IT ON IT AND NOBODY IN THAT MARKET SUGGESTED THAT IT OUGHT TO BE AND NOBODY WAS THANKED. IT IS ON THE BOARDS OF THE MARKET AND NOT ON THE WALL OF THE ROOM OVER IT, AND THE FITTING-OUT SHEET IS ON NO WALL IN THAT ROOM, AND THE TWO WERE NAMED SEPARATELY AND OUT LOUD IN THAT ROOM.**

**AND THE LOSS IS NOT WRITTEN AS A DEATH OF ANYTHING.** Nothing standing in that harbor moved. No man was paid. No price came down. Nobody had cheaper food. The four heads on that wall are the four heads. The party can no longer put a buoy where it wants one, can no longer be the people who go out to it, and can no longer be told what a route on that coast is doing, and that is on a page, in a yard's own mouth, and in the record of a room four hundred yards from that yard.

### The stage, taken once, in one chapter, and not improved afterwards

**CHAPTER 528, THURSDAY THE THIRTIETH, AND ONLY CHAPTER 528. THE WORD IS NOT IN ANY MOUTH ON ANY OF THE TEN DAYS, INCLUDING CHAPTERS 521 TO 527 AND 529 AND 530, AND NO CHAPTER DESCRIBES A THING THAT WOULD BECOME IT, AND NO PROTOTYPE WORK IS DONE IN THIS MOVEMENT.** Three men, each holding one channel of the same stretch of about four fathoms off that third lay, consented in their own mouths, tethered on lines of their own, one at a time.

**THE MECHANICS, ALL ON THE PAGE:** three slates written at about half past eleven in the morning before anybody was off that slip, each carrying the reason in that man's own words and the hour against it and **a figure of twenty-five minutes**; **THE THREE SLATES CARRY NO NAME, AND EACH IS SIGNED WITH A LAY AND A DATE AND AN HOUR, BEING THE TWENTY-NINTH OF DECEMBER AT ABOUT HALF PAST EIGHT, WHICH IS THE MORNING THE THREE OF THEM SAID THE WORDS OUT LOUD IN THAT SHED AND WERE ASKED IN THEM, AND NOT A DATE OUT OF ANY EARLIER MOVEMENT**; **AND THE THREE MEN OF THE FIRST LAY, THE WEST QUAY AND THE SECOND LAY ARE THREE MEN OF THIS HARBOR AND ARE NOT THE THREE MASTERS OF THE OSYRA, THE CORDLE AND THE SENNET, WHOSE NAMES ARE AT THE HEAD OF THE PAGE THAT WENT UP ON THE BOARDS OF THAT MARKET ON THE SUNDAY, AND THOSE THREE ARE FOUR DAYS DOWN THAT COAST**; **Ivo Sark, of about twenty-four, the named tender on the surface in a dinghy about nine feet off that slip, with his own hand on the chain weight and a cutoff he could pull without asking anybody's leave, and not in that water at any hour of that day**; **Nessa Pike, of about twenty-seven, on the compressor**; **the man who keeps the leaf was not the tender and said so out loud**; a setters mark put into a stone under about four fathoms on the twenty-first of December, which is an object on that floor and is a piece of lead in a hole in a stone and is not a person; a separate thirty feet of three-inch on its own weight for each man; one man in the water at a time; nobody in twice; nobody in at the top of that flood; and an ascent a man asked for was not argued with.

**THE PLAN ON THE BENCH STONE, AND IT IS NOT IN THREE EQUAL LENGTHS.** Two hundred yards of that water in three channels, one to a man, not measured against each other: the north one about ninety yards, the middle one about a hundred yards, and the south one a short piece nobody measured, at a float lying at about the two hundred yard mark with a bell under a board on it and the mark a Crown man set in a stone under it at about four fathoms on the twenty-first of December at the north end of that run. **THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-THREE WAS ASKED FOR THE NORTH ONE AND SAID YES, AND THE CHANNEL THAT WENT WAS THE NORTH ONE, SO THAT WHAT IS HELD IS THE MIDDLE ONE AND THE SHORT PIECE, BEING ABOUT A HUNDRED AND TEN YARDS, AND WHAT IS NOT HELD IS THE NORTH ONE, BEING ABOUT NINETY YARDS, WHICH IS WHERE THE FLOAT, THE MARK AND THE TROUGH ARE. 90 + 110 = 200 AND NOBODY WAS ASKED WHICH ONE WENT.**

EVERY DESCENT OF THAT DAY IS ON THE ONE THOUSAND ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY PENCE LINE OF AIR AND ON NO OTHER LINE, AND THE MAN WHO KEEPS THE LEAF SAID SO OUT LOUD BEFORE HE WROTE A FIGURE AGAINST IT.**

**THE CONSENT FAILURE, AND IT IS ON THE PAGE.** At about half past twelve in the afternoon, before anybody was off that slip, the man of about thirty-three of the west quay asked out loud for one of the three channels to be dropped. The drop was made on the slate with the hour against the rubbing-out. **Nobody argued with him about it, nobody asked him which channel it was, he was not thanked, and no figure is set against him. THE HELD WATER BECAME ABOUT A HUNDRED AND TEN YARDS OUT OF TWO HUNDRED, AND ABOUT NINETY YARDS AT THE NORTH END OF THAT STRETCH IS WATER NOBODY IN THAT HARBOR HAS LOOKED AT AND IS GOING TO STAY THAT WAY UNTIL SOMEBODY LOOKS AT IT, AND THE WHOLE PROOF OF THAT AFTERNOON IS WORTH LESS FOR IT.**

**THE RESULT, AND WHAT IT IS NOT.** Put together, about eleven fathoms of chain in a curve running north under the float into a trough about a foot and a half wide and about a foot deep with a setters mark in a stone over its north end, which is more than any one of those three men had. **It is not a recording, it is not a verdict, and it is not a route, and no part of it can be taken off a page by a stranger with a pencil because it is three men's mouths in a shed and not one page. THE THREE OF THEM DO NOT AGREE ABOUT ONE THING AND WERE KEPT DISAGREEING: WHETHER THAT FLOAT WAS BEING HELD BY ITS LINE OR WAS LOOSE IN THAT WATER. NOBODY SETTLED IT, IT WENT INTO THE SECOND COLUMN IN THE ORDER IT WAS SAID AND NOT INTO THE FIRST, AND THE MAN WHO KEEPS THE LEAF WAS ASKED FOR HIS OPINION AND SAID HE HAD NOT GOT ONE AND WAS NOT GOING TO GET ONE.**

**THE COST, IN THE SAME CHAPTER AND PAID IN THE SAME CHAPTER.** At about six o'clock in the evening all three of them said out loud, in three mouths at once, that they had the same thing: a sweetness at the back of the throat, a pressure behind the eyes that was not a headache, and a want to be quiet that went off of its own accord in about ten minutes. It was not a lesson and it was not a speech and nobody was thanked and no figure is set against it and none of the three is a member of anything. **AND AT ABOUT TEN TO SEVEN THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO, WHO KEPT THE BOOK AND THE THREE SLATES AND THE HOURS AND WHO WAS NOT THE TENDER AND WHO WAS NOT IN THAT WATER AT ANY HOUR OF THAT AFTERNOON, SAID OUT LOUD, TO ABOUT NINE MEN, THAT HE WAS NOT CERTAIN WHICH OF THE THREE ACCOUNTS WAS HIS OWN, AND SAID IT IN ABOUT TWENTY WORDS AND DID NOT EXPLAIN IT AND NOBODY ASKED HIM TO. THAT IS NOT IMPROVED IN THIS VOLUME, NO FIGURE IS SET AGAINST IT, HE IS NOT A CASUALTY, NOBODY HAS NAMED HIM ONE, AND HE IS NOT A MAN WHO HAS BEEN IN THE WATER TOO OFTEN.**

**AND ON THE THIRTY-FIRST THE AFTERTASTE HAD NOT LIFTED, ONE OF THE THREE SAID OUT LOUD IT WAS NOT GETTING BETTER AND WAS NOT GETTING WORSE AND THAT HE HAD STOPPED EXPECTING IT TO, AND NOBODY ASKED HIM WHAT IT WAS LIKE, NOBODY WROTE A FIGURE AGAINST IT, AND NOBODY IN THAT HARBOR HAS MADE IT LIFT AND IT IS NOT A CONDITION ANYBODY THERE IS GOING TO FIX. THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO HAS SAID THE ONE SENTENCE ONCE AND HAS NOT BEEN ASKED ABOUT IT SINCE AND NOBODY IN THAT HARBOR HAS SAID A WORD ABOUT IT TO HIM.**

### The checks, run after the writing and recorded as counts and not as assertions

**ARITHMETIC. THE NINE OUT-LINES WERE ADDED AND EVERY FIGURE WAS CHECKED.** 2,400 + 672 + 2,400 + 1,120 + 1,280 + 672 + 960 + 336 + 1,120 = **10,960 pence, being sixty-eight marks, six shillings and eightpence**, and 68 × 160 + 6 × 12 + 8 = 10,960. 47,538 + 10,960 = 58,498 and 58,498 − 10,640 = 47,858. **EVERY DISTINCT FIGURE-OF-MONEY-AND-GLOSS PAIR ON THE TEN PAGES WAS EXTRACTED BY A SCRIPT AND EVALUATED ON ONE MARK TO ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY PENCE, AND ALL NINETY-EIGHT DISTINCT PAIRS EVALUATE, INCLUDING THE FIGURES CARRIED OVER FROM CHAPTERS 501 TO 520 WHICH WERE RUN IN THE SAME PASS.** The two figures that are new to this movement and that are most likely to fail are the fifty-eight thousand four hundred and ninety-eight, which is 365 marks and eighteen pence, and the forty-seven thousand eight hundred and fifty-eight, which is 299 marks and eighteen pence, **and eighteen pence is one shilling and sixpence in both, not one shilling and twopence, and both are printed as one shilling and sixpence on the page.** The running out and the shortfall on all ten days were derived by adding from the base of Chapter 520 and compared with the figure printed on the face of each of the ten pages, and ten of ten agree.

**CLOCKS. THE THREE CLOCKS OF THE THIRTIETH WERE RUN AGAINST THEMSELVES AND ALL THREE CLOSE AT EVERY FIGURE: 25 minutes in the water each, 5 + 18 + 2 = 25 of the 25 on the slate, the windows 1:10 to 1:35, 2:10 to 2:35 and 3:10 to 3:35 with no overlap, the last helmet off at about thirty-five minutes past three and the top of the flood at about five o'clock.** The derived figures on the page were also run: 110 held yards + 90 yards not looked at = 200; 298 + 262 = 560 in Chapter 529; 2,400 − 1,600 = 800 and 2,400 − 2,240 = 160 and 2,240 − 1,600 = 640 in Chapter 521; 2,400 + 672 = 3,072 = nineteen marks two shillings and eightpence; 1,280 + 672 = 1,952 = twelve marks two shillings and eightpence.

**COUNTED DOCUMENTS, AND EVERY ONE OF THEM PASSES.** The eleven words of Chapter 523 are eleven; the four lines on the record are four; the four lines of the buoys list are four and carry five marks; the five sentences at the head of the page in Chapter 527 are five; the three slates in Chapter 528 are three; the three questions in Chapter 529 are three; the five lines of the page read out in Chapter 530 are five.

**THE DUPLICATION SWEEP WAS RUN ACROSS ALL FORTY-FIVE PAIRS OF THE TEN SECOND COLUMNS AND ACROSS ALL ONE HUNDRED PAIRS BETWEEN THE TEN AND THE SECOND COLUMNS OF CHAPTERS 501 TO 520, WITH THE HOUSE'S OWN APPARATUS ENTRY FORMULA, THE ATTRIBUTION FORMULA, AND THE PROMPT'S OWN EXEMPTION PHRASES STRIPPED OUT OF BOTH ENDS OF EVERY PAIR. IT WAS HUNG AND SEATED ON FOUR PADS OF SAWN FIR AT ABOUT TEN PAST FOUR IN THE AFTERNOON OF THE THIRTY-FIRST DAY OF OCTOBER PAST AND HAS STOOD WHERE IT STANDS SINCE THAT DAY, BEING CHAPTER 469, AND NOT THE EIGHTH OF NOVEMBER, WHICH A FIRST DRAFT OF CHAPTER 494 PRINTED AND WHICH WAS REPAIRED.**

### The strip

**Chapter 491.** A plain riveted bell about five foot across and four foot high, open at the bottom, goes down onto a ring beside the last of fifteen frames at about half past eight and three men go down in it one at a time on the boat's own bottles, not on a line, under a figure of forty minutes on each slate, with Ivo Sark of about twenty-four named as the tender on the surface and not in the bell and a cutoff he could pull without asking. **Ollum Trevask, of about thirty-four, of the second lay, 9.10 to 9.50.** **Sabra Loach, of about thirty-one, who crews nothing and sells nothing, 10.10 to 10.50**, and who says one thing about her own body and not one thing about what is in the room, and who comes up with a taste like a penny that had been in a pipe and is not told what she gave it. **A man of about thirty-seven, 11.10 to 11.50**, and who worked the pump that afternoon. Nobody is thanked. At about twelve minutes past nine the tender says out loud that the man in that bell is not answering and **nobody pulls the cutoff, because a man who has stopped answering has not asked to come up and the whole of the house's rule is that a man asks**; he begins answering again at about thirty-one minutes and asks to come up, and the cutoff is pulled without asking anybody anything.

### The anchor

**Chapter 492, and it is on a clock that closes in four places.** **THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-SEVEN GOES DOWN AT ABOUT TEN PAST ONE ON A SLATE OF HIS OWN WITH HIS OWN REASON AND THE HOUR AGAINST IT, IS OUT OF THAT BELL AND ON THAT FLOOR AT ABOUT HALF PAST ONE, AND IS IN THE WATER FORTY MINUTES. THE HOLDER OF THAT WRIT GOES INTO THE SAME BELL AT ABOUT A QUARTER PAST ONE, IS SEATED IN THE ELEVENTH FRAME AT ABOUT HALF PAST ONE, AND IS IN THE WATER THIRTY-FIVE MINUTES. THE TENDER SAYS AT ABOUT THIRTY-FIVE MINUTES PAST ONE THAT THE MAN ON THAT FLOOR IS NOT ANSWERING. THE WORD COMES AT ABOUT FORTY-ONE MINUTES PAST ONE, WHICH IS ELEVEN MINUTES AFTER THE HALF HOUR. THE CUTOFF IS PULLED WITHOUT ANYBODY ASKING. THE BELL IS UP IN ABOUT SIX MINUTES AND BOTH OF THEM ARE OUT OF THAT WATER AT ABOUT TEN TO TWO.** One bell, one man in it at a time, two bodies on that floor at the eleventh frame and the front of those frames, the machine taking from both, and what it took from the man at the frames coming through that frame and into him. **Nobody asked him. The man who keeps the leaf said the one thing that was said out loud about it and said it once: that a person who is asked whether he will be used as a piece of equipment has already been used as one.** He comes up with an aftertaste that did not lift, a tremor in both hands that is still in them on the second day of December, and a stretch of his own afternoon from about two to about four that he cannot put in order and that Nessa Pike has in the minute with the hour against each. **No figure is set against any part of it anywhere, he is not a casualty, nobody has named him one, nobody thanked him, nobody was asked to be thanked and he is not an example of anything and was not made one.** He is not a man who goes into twenty-two fathoms again in this volume, and he says so out loud once on the twenty-fifth.

### The cache, and the hour it was put back

**Chapter 493, and this is `outline/volume-10.md` § *Volume climax* element two, and it is on the page.** The cache came up on the fourteenth in three baskets, went into the crate on the twenty-second, and the crate stood battened on that after deck with the batten that was put on it in that yard's own mouth on the thirty-first day of October past and has not been off since. **At about eleven in the morning on the twenty-fifth the holder of that writ says it out loud, in front of all nine of them, before he has said a word to anybody about it, and he says it once, and it takes about four minutes: that he is leaving it; that it is the best evidence this party has ever had in its hands and he is leaving it in the dark on the bottom of a trench in a room behind a machine three of them cannot agree about; that it is also the only thing in that room that holds a route together, and that any man alive can come back to that room with that paper in it, and that the day it is in a crate on a boat that room is a hole in a floor with nothing in it; that the paper goes to the room and not to the boat and the crate on that deck comes up empty; that the brown page under the weight on that tarpaulin comes up flat and goes on no sheet of any kind; and that he is not using that room to decide where that boat goes, and that the boat sails on the morrow at about four in the afternoon whatever is on that floor and whatever is on that deck.** Nobody argued with him, nobody thanked him, nobody was asked to agree with him, nobody was asked whether he had thought about it, and the whole of it went into the second column with the hour of eleven o'clock against it.

**AND THEN IT IS CARRIED BACK DOWN AND PUT BACK WHERE IT WAS.** The crate is taken forward off that after deck at about half past eleven, still battened, and set down by the fore hatch. The man of about fifty-one and the man of about thirty-seven go down at about ten past one on air of the twenty-fourth, forty minutes apiece, with the crate roped to a line and the three baskets roped inside it, one man in that bell at a time, and both of them out of that water at about ten to two. **On that floor the batten comes off, the three baskets come out one at a time, and they go back onto the second shelf of the rack against the back wall on the north side of that room, in the dark, in the places they had been in.** A line is added to the end of one of the two slates left inside that doorway on the eleventh of November, being that the room behind the wall and the paper in it stay as they are and that the party is not coming back for them, with the hour of the twenty-fifth of November against it and nothing else, and nobody told either man what to write. **The batten goes back across the lid before the crate is hauled up, and the crate comes up in that bell empty and goes into the forepeak, and it is in that forepeek on the twenty-seventh, and it is off that deck on the second day of December, and it is the closing image.**

**THE ONE DAMP PAGE IS NOT IN THAT CRATE AND NEVER WAS.** It is the third thing off that same second shelf, it lay flat under a weight on a tarpaulin on the after deck from the fourteenth to the twenty-seventh, it was not cut, it was not folded, it is on no sheet in that boat and on no sheet in that harbor, and it went up to a room over that market flat on a board with a weight on it and did not go into the case. A woman of thirty of no office is the only person who knows exactly where it is and has said so out loud once.

### The proof

**Chapter 494, Friday the twenty-sixth.** A man of about fifty-one goes down at about ten past ten, is in the water about ten minutes and in that bell and on that floor about thirty of them, and comes up at about ten to eleven with one whole sheet, folded twice, about nine inches by six, not cut and not wet. **It was not in that room with the racks. It was about four foot off it, on the other side, against the north wall, under a lid, in a bundle of about forty sheets tied with a cord that had gone to a hard grey colour, and he put the other thirty-nine back and put the cord back as he found it.** On the face of it: a head with a rule under it and six short strokes ruled down the left of the body; a place, being the name of a port and not the name of that harbor; a date, being the fourteenth day of a month that the clerk of that office called by a name this coast does not use; **no year at all, and that is not a thing that has been taken off it, the year of that office having been kept in a register in another building**; a line ruled about two inches long with nothing on it in ink, with **beside its middle an impression pressed into the paper about the size of a thumbnail, broken at the top edge by a fold that goes through it, the two sides of the impression not making up into one another**; at the foot, in a second and larger hand in an ink brown where the first is black, an endorsement of one line and a rule under it and **a name, being Ilya Serr, an examiner of that office, the office being the one whose engineers rebuilt the frame on that floor three hundred years after a man of about thirty-four said out loud that the frame under the fittings was six centuries old**; and down the left margin, in a third hand in a green ink, four words and a short stroke, being that the sheet was received into that port's ferry file. **Three hands, three inks, three dates, and a stranger with a leaf and a pencil can take all three off the face of the paper in about a minute and find that they are three and not two.** The word *plate* is not used of any of it and the second element of the three named at `outline/series.md` is a pressed impression and not a plate, and no plate in eleven feet is reached, measured, touched, asked about or named in any of these ten chapters.

**AND THE FOUR LIMITS ARE SAID OUT LOUD ON THE DECK IN THE OPEN AT ABOUT TWO IN THE AFTERNOON, IN THE HOLDER'S OWN MOUTH, AND ARE RECORDED IN THE MINUTE WITH THE HOUR AGAINST THEM.** It does not show why, and there is no line of writing anywhere on that sheet with a reason at the head of it. It does not show that the man whose name is on it knew what was in the case, and there is nothing whatever on the face of that paper about what was in the case. It does not name anybody as the author of a lie and it is not a confession. **It is a piece of paper. It does not consent, it cannot be asked anything, and it does not testify.** Calder Marr stopped the one sentence that was going to get itself into a record and put four lines under it, and the man of about fifty-one said he would not argue, and the whole of the four were read back to him word for word off the holder's own slate before he went below. That boat got under way at about four in the afternoon.

**Chapter 495, Saturday the twenty-seventh.** A case, a lock and a lining of oilcloth at three hundred and twenty pence, being two marks, with the twenty-seventh against it. **The man who keeps the leaf said out loud before he wrote the line that it was the case and not the crate, that the crate is a different thing and is not on that line and is not coming into that harbor in anybody's hand, and that nobody was to write a second line under it that week saying what is going to be put in it.** The sheet went into that case at about two in the afternoon **in a room over that fish market**, with the lock shut afterward and the key in the keeping of the woman who wrote the minute, and nobody in that harbor read it and nobody was shown it and nobody was asked what it said. **Sabra Loach, of about thirty-one, who crews nothing and sells nothing, put it in and said one sentence while she was doing it: that a case is a thing that can be carried and a case is not a hand, and a thing in a hand is a thing one man has, and this is a thing a room has.** The master of that boat came ashore with his two men and his boy and was not thanked and was asked nothing and gave no date and his boat is not put to sea again on any day of that trip.

**Chapter 499, Wednesday the first day of December.** **The case was opened in a room over that fish market at about ten past two in the afternoon and not in a shed**, by the woman who wrote the minute, who had had the key in her keeping since the twenty-seventh and who had not had anybody ask her for it in the four days between. **She put her hand flat on the paper for a moment and took it off and did not lift it out of the case with her own hands.** Hobb Lee, of about forty-six, who mends nets on the third lay, read the paper out at about twenty past two and again at about half past two with his own name and the hour under each, nobody stopped him at any word, **the four limits were read out with it and not after it, so that about eleven people who cannot read heard the paper, then all four of the limits, and then the paper again**, and the order went into the record that room keeps. **There is no man at the head of that table and no head on any sheet in that room and nobody in that room is only ever a name or a seal or an office.** A man of about forty asked out loud whether the man whose name was on it was a bad man, and a woman of thirty of no office answered him, and was not thanked, and said that a signature on a transfer is a signature on a transfer, that this one settles nothing, that it does not say what he thought when he signed it, and that she is not going to hand a room of people who cannot read a worse man than the paper has got. A record of the reading went into the book of that room, the paper went back into the case, the case was locked and the key went back.

### The room over a fish market, and the four lines, and the no

**Chapter 496, Sunday the twenty-eighth.** The wall behind a reeve's bench came down bare for the eighty-second time and went up unrepaired at the angle it has been at since the twelfth. The room was let out on that Sunday, a bowl went down on the step, and about twenty people went up in the half hour after two o'clock and about eleven of them could not read. **The man who keeps the leaf stood where the long table is and said out loud at about ten minutes to two that neither the sheet that carries the money nor the first column of that leaf nor the second of it is in that room or on any wall in it**, and that anybody who wants either of the two things said out loud in a room like that one can ask for it, and that it will not be that afternoon. **Hobb Lee read out twice a sheet written the day before in the hand of Nessa Pike, of about twenty-seven of that yard, being the account of what was done in that harbor on the twenty-seventh and what was not done in it**, with the rule on the face of the paper above the account: the reader's own name goes under what he reads and the hour under his name, and anybody in that room may stop him at any word and put their own words against his, and what goes into the book afterward is what is on the paper. Readings at **two o'clock and twenty-five minutes past two**. Nobody stopped him in the first. **In the second, at about half past two, at one word in the ninth line, a man of about fifty-one out of a coast town four days down said that is fifty, and said that he counted them on the hatch head on the Tuesday before they came away and counted them twice, and that there were about forty of them in the bundle and not fifty, and would give the trade and the years and the hour against the correction and not the name, because he would rather a man who thinks the figure is wrong came down that hatch and counted them himself than had his name on a paper in a harbor where he has never worked. The wrong figure was left where it was, not rubbed out, not scraped, not taken off with a knife, and he was not asked for a name.** Hobb Lee read the ninth line again exactly as it was written, so that the people at the back heard the wrong figure a second time and knew what was being argued at, and then read the whole sheet out a third time from the top with the correction under the ninth line.

**Chapter 497, Monday the twenty-ninth.** A man of about fifty who owns a boat of about twenty-two tons, who wrote a thing on the wall of that room on the tenth of October past and has not said the name of it since, proposed out loud at about ten past three **that there be a roll of the people who put nothing in, not to move them but to stop them being asked again.** A ropemaker of about sixty-one, who is not in her room on a Sunday and has not been in one for two years, said no in about four words from about nine feet back: **there is no roll.** She said that somebody will be asked twice, and yes, and a man in this room in six weeks will be able to say to that person, you said no to me once, in a room, and I have a paper, and it will be true, and it will be worse than being asked cold, and it will be worse for them than it is now because now it is one man with a bad memory and afterwards it is a room with a sheet — and **I put nothing in**, not one penny of hers is on that sheet on any line and nobody asked her for one and nobody asked her twice, and she came up those stairs anyway, because a man who wants a list of us ought to be made to stand up in the room with the rest of you and be told no to his face rather than go home and write it out. **The holder of that writ said the only other thing that was said about it: that it was no in this room on this day and not in a shed, that the two of them are the holder of that writ and a ropemaker of about sixty-one, that is all that goes in the minute about it, that it is not going to be the fourth thing on that table, and that he is not going to ask this room to hold a list of the people it has not got anything from. Nobody wrote anything. There is no such roll in that room, there is none in that harbor, and none is going to be.** Later that afternoon a man at the front of that room put one question to Ollum Trevask about whether the thing in a case is going on that wall, and got **no**, and a second question about why not, and was told that there was not going to be a why, that he had said no to the putting of it on the wall and that was the whole of it, and **ask me about the rope.** Nobody asked him about the rope.

**Chapter 498, Tuesday the thirtieth, the fifty-eighth wage Tuesday.** The wage column did not move and a further week stands fallen due and that is the fifty-eighth week of it. **At about two in the afternoon the holder of that writ stood in that room in front of about twenty people, about eleven of whom cannot read, with a sheet of four lines in his own hand in his coat, and he said it first, out loud, before anybody had asked him anything:** that he was going to read the four lines himself, that he wrote them on Saturday night in a shed, **that the man who got the thing they are about is a man of about fifty-one out of a coast town four days down who is in that harbor and is not at that table and did not write a word of them, that what he is claiming is not that he carried it up out of that room**, and that he sat in the eleventh frame on that floor on the Wednesday for about eleven minutes and held a man there with his own back, and that if a man in that harbor hears four sentences about a floor that was twenty-two fathoms down read out by the man who sat in it, those four sentences carry something they would not carry out of a man who mends nets. **Hobb Lee put his thumb between the pages of the long table's own book and said no in one sentence: that a man who reads out a thing he has a stake in cannot be stopped by anybody standing in the room, and that in this room the whole of the power to stop him is one word, and the word is that you are reading it straight, and that word is not a stop, and that it is asking them to trust him and asking a person who cannot read to check him is asking them to do the thing they came because they cannot do.** And then: **in September a page in an office on a hill was worth a room. That is the whole of what a page is worth and it is not nothing.** The holder named it as the hole in the rule he said out loud on the sixth of November and did not argue with a man who has never argued with him about anything. Hobb Lee said: **I know you are not going to argue. That is the reason it was easy to say it.** The holder sat down on the bench at the back of that room at about ten past three and put the sheet on the long table face down. **He was not thanked for standing in that room and the room was not satisfied and nobody in it said that anything had been settled.** Hobb Lee wrote his own name and the hour under each of the four lines as he read them, being the hours of ten past three, of a quarter past three and of twenty minutes to four, stopped after each one and looked round the room, and nobody put a hand up and nobody said a word against any of them. A woman at the back who cannot read put her hand up about halfway through the second and had it read again exactly the same. **The name on each of the four is his own, there are four of them and they are the same name, and he was not restored by any of them and did not ask to be.** A man of about fifty who owns a boat of about twenty-two tons looked at the sheet for a while and said out loud that the four heads on that wall had not changed by any of it and that a fifth head was not going to be added to that wall by anybody on account of a Tuesday. **The four questions people in that harbor asked a man in a hall on the west basin in the spring were not asked in that room and were not answered in it.**

### The close, and the question

**Chapter 500, Thursday the second day of December, a rota day, the hundred and fourth charge on that cistern, walked on by none of it.** **At about ten past five in the evening, on that after deck, in the open, in the ship's own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, the leaf was read back and read twice because about four men of that party cannot read, and both definitions came out of the same mouth in the same words they came out of on the twenty-second of October past and the first, eleventh and twenty-second of November, and the reading prints its own arithmetic on its own face.** The reading is at **two hundred and thirty-two and one thousand and thirty-seven at that hour and two hundred and thirty-three and one thousand and thirty-nine at the close of that day**, and the printed derivation is **five a day on fifty days is two hundred and fifty, two hundred and forty-five of those went in on the forty-nine days before this one and three went in this morning before this hour, two hundred and fifty less two is two hundred and forty-eight, and seven hundred and eighty-nine and two hundred and forty-eight is one thousand and thirty-seven**, and the span sentence is the repaired Chapter 490 form: **fifty have gone in on the fifty days of the fifty-one from Wednesday the thirteenth of October to this day, one against each of them, and not one day in two of them, there being one day in between that is the twelfth day of November and that is a day nobody is in.** The third column is empty and nobody has been appointed to it and the hand of a boy of twenty-two is at the head of it and his surname is on no page and **that boy is not on the water and nobody has asked him why.** The fourth column has one hundred and twenty-five lines at that hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close, has taken no line in these fifty days, has no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, **and that is not a closure and it is not a strike-out and nobody has closed that column and nobody in that yard is going to.** The sheet that carries the money is then read back in full with the day against every line, carrying no count of persons, the three who said no at the same size as the figures, and all eight of the movement's out-lines read out one by one: **bread and salt beef for nine men for ten days 1,600, a day apiece in advance to the same four men 672, four days of coal for the pump 2,352, five fresh days of air 900, a second pair of hands for a day 168, a case a lock and a lining of oilcloth 320, a boat of about nineteen tons five days under way 1,250, and a day apiece to the same four men 672 — seven thousand nine hundred and thirty-four pence, being forty-nine marks, seven shillings and tenpence** — and **twenty-one thousand nine hundred and ten pence short, being one hundred and thirty-six marks, twelve shillings and sixpence, against that yard's own book and nobody's else, and it was said out loud in that yard's own mouth and no figure has been asked of any person in that harbor to make it otherwise.**

**AND THEN, AT ABOUT TWENTY TO SIX IN THE EVENING, AT THE HEAD OF THAT MOLE, IN THE DARK, WITH THE LIGHT ON IT OUT AND ITS LENS OUT SINCE THE SEVENTH OF MAY AND THE WIND OFF THE LAND AND COLD, ABOUT ELEVEN PEOPLE STANDING, A WOMAN OF ABOUT FIFTY-EIGHT WITH AN END STALL AND A SLATE PUT HER SLATE AGAINST THE PARAPET AND ASKED IT ONCE:**

> **If they are putting that old thing back together on that floor down there, how many harbors have to be joined up to it before a man can make it work?**

**NOBODY ANSWERED IT.** The holder of that writ was about nine feet off her and did not answer it. The woman of thirty of no office did not answer it. The man of about fifty with the boat of about twenty-two tons did not answer it. A man of about thirty-four, who has a hole in the middle of a Tuesday, did not answer it and was not asked it. A man of about twenty-nine stood at the front and did not hear it asked and nobody told him he had. **Nessa Pike entered it in that minute as asked, with the hour of twenty to six in the evening of the second day of December against it, and read it back to the woman who asked it, and the woman who asked it did not ask to have it read back and did not ask for a word of it to be changed. IT HAS NOT BEEN ASKED A SECOND TIME IN THAT HARBOR AND IS NOT GOING TO BE, AND THERE IS NO ANSWER TO IT ANYWHERE ON THAT COAST THAT NIGHT, AND THE PERSON WHO ASKED IT DID NOT ASK IT TO BE ANSWED THAT NIGHT.**

**THE COUNT OF THAT QUESTION, AND OF ANY FORM OF IT, ACROSS CHAPTERS 491 TO 499 IS ZERO AND ACROSS 491 TO 500 IT IS ONE. IT IS IN ONE MOUTH. IT NAMES NO PERSON.**

### The money, re-derived by adding

**NOTHING WENT INTO THAT SHEET IN ANY HAND ON ANY OF THESE TEN DAYS AND THIS MOVEMENT ASKED NOBODY FOR ANYTHING.** What went out was on eight lines and is **7,934 pence, being forty-nine marks, seven shillings and tenpence.** The base at the close of Chapter 490 was 10,640 in and 24,616 out. The running out across the ten days is **26,888 / 30,308 / 30,308 / 30,308 / 30,628 / 30,628 / 31,878 / 32,550 / 32,550 / 32,550**, and the shortfalls are **16,248 / 19,668 / 19,668 / 19,668 / 19,988 / 19,988 / 21,238 / 21,910 / 21,910 / 21,910**, every one of them evaluating on one mark to one hundred and sixty pence. **The bag stands at twenty-eight pence at the close of every one of the ten days, being two shillings and fourpence, short of the wage of four marks by six hundred and twelve pence, being three marks eleven shillings, and it is never zero; one hundred and sixty-eight pence came into that yard and one hundred and sixty-eight went out of it on each of the ten days, the whole of the ten being one thousand six hundred and eighty pence each way, being ten marks, six shillings and eightpence; and not one penny of the whole of that trip's cost came out of that bag, out of the owner of any boat, out of the man with two papers or out of the Crown, and the deficit at the end of this movement comes out of that yard's own book.** The sheet carries no count of persons and the three who said no stand on it at the same size as the contributions and **none of the three was asked again in this movement.**

### The nine day-counts, and the twelfth day of November

**AT THE CLOSE OF CHAPTER 490 AND ON THE *n*TH DAY OF THIS BATCH EVERY ONE OF THOSE NINE IS ITS OWN FIGURE PLUS *n*. NINETY COUNTS WERE RE-EXTRACTED FROM THE TEN STANDING PARAGRAPHS AND COMPARED WITH THEIR OWN BASE PLUS THEIR OWN DAY AFTER THE REPAIRS, AND NINETY OF NINETY AGREE.** The base is 188 / 190 / 528 / 294 / 112 / 67 / 82 / 99 / 130 and the twenty-second of November itself reads 189 / 191 / 529 / 295 / 113 / 68 / 83 / 100 / 131. The four-column span is **fifty-one calendar days from Wednesday the thirteenth of October to Thursday the second day of December, carrying fifty entries, of which the one day nobody is in is the twelfth day of November.** The figure of five hundred and fifty-eight pence that `outline/volume-10.md` L4 fixes is Movement 1's against Movement 1's two lines and **is ruled and is not printed in any of these ten chapters.**

### What the volume closes on, and what it does not close

**IT DOES NOT CLOSE ON ANYTHING PAID, ADVANCED, REDUCED, IMPROVED, STRUCK OR CLOSED.** The mole-head light is out and its lens has been out since the seventh of May. The north berth is out. The hose is dead until the spring. The tide gang is four men short. The hard at Ashtide is unanswered. One berth is short on the third lay. Nineteen winters are disputed and unpaid. There is no flour in that market and none is coming this month, no barley since the middle of September, no barrel of lamp oil since the twenty-ninth of August, and a figure of four hundred and fifty pence still on a board at an end stall that did not come down. There is no physic at fourteen pence and none of it. The wage column stands at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks with twenty envelopes in a chest and a further week fallen due at every wage Tuesday. **The cistern was charged for the hundred and first, second, third and fourth times in this volume and walked on at every charge.** The third column is empty, unappointed, with a boy's hand at the head of it and his surname on no page and the boy off the water. The four heads on the wall have not changed. **The harbor is poorer on the second day of December than on the thirteenth day of October and that is the whole of the cost.**

**IT CLOSES ON A MACHINE SIX CENTURIES OLD STANDING ON THE BOTTOM OF A TRENCH IN ABOUT TWENTY-FATHOMS UNDER A BELL-SHAPED CHAMBER WITH A STOVE IN IT AND A STOVE DRAWN OUT AND A HATCH SHUT, WITH CROWN MAN'S MARKS SET AROUND IT, AND NOBODY IN THAT HARBOR GIVEN THAT MACHINE AND NOBODY IN THAT HARBOR STOPPED FROM KNOWING ABOUT IT; ON A ROOM ON THAT FLOOR BEHIND IT THAT STILL HOLDS THE ONLY COPY OF THE BEST EVIDENCE THIS PARTY EVER HAD; ON A HOLE IN THE MIDDLE OF A TUESDAY; ON AN AFTERTASTE AND TWO HANDS THAT ARE NOT STEADY ON THE SECOND DAY OF DECEMBER; ON A MAN WHO WILL NOT HEAR OUT OF THE LEFT SIDE OF HIS HEAD UNTIL THE FOURTH DAY OF DECEMBER, WHICH IS AFTER THIS VOLUME; AND ON A QUESTION ASKED ONCE AT A MOLE HEAD AND ANSWERED BY NOBODY.**

### Locks this batch hands to the Volume 10 close and to Volume 11

1. **The cache is on the bottom of that trench, in the racks, in the dark, in three baskets on the second shelf of the rack against the back wall on the north side of that room, in the places they had been in. It is the only copy. Any man alive can come back to that room with that paper in it. A later volume may not say that it came up, and may not put a copy of it in a room, a record or a hand.**
2. **The crate came up empty with the batten back across its lid and is in that boat's forepeak, and there is no word on any page of that harbor for what was going to be in it. The two crates are not the same crate and are not to be counted together.**
3. **The brown page is in a room over that fish market, flat, on a board, under a weight, cut by nobody, on no sheet, and a woman of thirty of no office is the only person who knows exactly where it is.**
4. **The proof is a single whole sheet in a case with a lock and a lining of oilcloth, in a room over a fish market, with four limits on the face of the reading, in a record that a room keeps, and it names nobody as the author of a lie. It is not a confession and it is not a verdict.**
5. **The question was asked once, on the second day of December, at about twenty to six in the evening, at a mole head, in a woman of about fifty-eight's mouth, naming no person, answered by nobody, entered in a minute as asked, and not asked again anywhere in fifty chapters. No later volume may re-ask it in the same words and no later volume may answer it.**
6. **The strip is paid, the anchor is paid, the cache is paid, the proof is paid and the question is paid. The Keelwright stage was taken in Volume 09 and is not taken again. The Chorus Diver stage is Volume 11's and was not entered here; the count of *chorus* across Volume 10 is one and it is in Chapter 473.**
